claims.text: The baseline condition is a comparatively coarse-grained FeNiCrCoCu HEA coating on a conventional metal substrate.
A controlled annealing or thermomechanical treatment can refine the FeNiCrCoCu coating grains relative to the baseline.
Reducing grain size increases the coating's grain-boundary density.
Increasing grain-boundary density will improve the high-temperature wear resistance of the FeNiCrCoCu coating.
Grain refinement will shift microscopic deformation from dislocation accumulation toward grain-boundary sliding.
Grain boundaries act as barriers to dislocation motion in the coating.
A higher grain-boundary density limits dislocation accumulation and promotes more uniform grain-boundary sliding.
More uniform grain-boundary sliding reduces localized plastic deformation.
Reduced localized plastic deformation leads to a lower high-temperature sliding wear rate.
The grain-refined coating will have greater hardness and resistance to plastic flow than the coarse-grained baseline.
The coarse-grained baseline has higher wear because of localized dislocation accumulation and less effective plastic-deformation accommodation.
The predicted behavior should hold during sliding at temperatures of approximately 700°C or higher, provided the refined microstructure remains stable.
Sufficiently high temperature can cause grain growth or phase transformations that eliminate the predicted grain-refinement benefit.
Elemental segregation or secondary-phase formation at grain boundaries could alter the magnitude of the wear-resistance improvement.
Failure to obtain a statistically significant wear reduction together with no shift toward grain-boundary-mediated deformation, or observation of increased wear, would falsify the hypothesis.
